Portland experiential technology pros, how the heck did none of you tell me about CETI?!? 🤬

If you don't know CETI, they are a non-profit organization that focuses on emerging technologies, creative workshops, and interactive public art exhibits.

I got to take a tour of their new space, and MY GOODNESS Y'ALL!!! It's basically an experience agency that you can use for free.

Let me say that again: this is all of the hardware of an experience agency that, somehow, you can use...

...for free.

Want VR helmets? They've got that.
3D printers? Covered.
Soldering tools? Of course.
NUCs? Yup.
Projectors? Yuuuuuup.
Tablets? Duh.
LED Walls? More like Y-E-S walls.

Think about how lucky we are to have these folks in our city. I mean, I'm looking around the room and I see recreational creative techs, pros, networkers, connecters - folks of all types, connected by a neon strobing chain: 

The passion we all have for creative technology. 🔥

So I'm hooked. I can't wait to see what I can do to help this community out. The opportunities CETI gives folks can only be replicated by college or work experience, typically, and I'll say this louder for the folks in the back:

IT'S FREE!!!

There will be another meeting in August to talk about the art show they'll be having later on in the year. I think there are real opportunities for local pros and their companies to get involved and make a huge impact on the local community. I believe this could have a ripple effect that would help PDX get its experiential tech swagger back.

If you haven’t seen experiential software come to life on production hardware for the first time, you haven’t lived. 

No, seriously. There’s no time to wait. 

Go quit your job now. Take out student loans. Graduate with honors from NYU. Break into the industry. Work with your new teammates deep in the intersection of design and technology, building bespoke software that pushes the limits of how man and machine interact. 

Then, when you’re on site and surrounded by your peers and clients, waiting with baited breath as you toil and configure for hours, know that it’ll all be worth it if you can just get everything to work in-sync. 

Wait — was that what I think it was?

Did everything finally start working like it always has on your local machine?

That beating in your chest isn’t stress or excitement. No, it’s so much more than that.

Congratulations. This is what you’ve been working towards for years.

Now you’re truly alive.

Folks, I'm honored and humbled to share with you all that last week I was presented with a Community Award from Fireside. 🥹

In February, I saw on Instagram that Bryant Place would be giving a presentation at a creative technology meetup, and my interest was piqued. A creative tech meetup in town? Awesome - sign me up!

So I show up, watch the incredible presentations, and get to chatting with Terence, the organizer of the event. I’m immediately hooked. The vision was clear: build and highlight the creative technology community in Portland. As someone who had been working in the field for five years, I felt like this was something I could contribute to by leveraging my professional connections and helping grow our group’s resources.

To top it all off, Bryant’s presentation was about how the CMS software I build adds value to immersive experiences. I was so ready to Kool-Aid Man myself through the wall and build the best damn experiential CMS I possibly could.

The very next month, I was laid off from that job...

Next Fireside in April, I show up, unemployed and lost. Frankly, I didn't feel like I had anything to contribute anymore.

However, being at Fireside really kept my soul warm. While I was there, I saw folks from all sorts of creative backgrounds coming together to learn and build - but more importantly, I saw people supporting one another. The community was there to act as an emotional safety net for folks who needed it.

So I’m telling you all this to say: this award means a hell of a lot more to me than I can begin to express. It represents a year that started about as rough as it could and is ending with uncertainty, but also with copious amounts of hope.

I'm not crying, you're crying. 
---

While I have your attention, Fireside will be looking for a few things next year as we continue to grow as a community:

1. We're looking for presenters!
If you’ve got wisdom to share, we’d love to hear it. We’re especially excited to have PDX-based presenters speak at our in-person Fireside meetups, but we’ll also be starting virtual meetups so anyone can be part of the group. If you want to chat about creative ideas, technology, AI, business - or even how to run a group like ours - let’s freaking talk and get you in. Plus, it’s a great way to put yourself out there and add presenting to your resume.

2. We're looking for corporate sponsors!
Sponsorships start at $50/month and really help us make these events happen. We’ll work with you and your organization to make sure you’re getting the most bang for your buck. Don't let Bracket Bear beat y'all to the punch here.

3. We're looking for other venues to host the event at.
Ideally, we’re looking for a place with a big ol’ LED wall (potentially called a “Big Wall?”) that we can rip some presentations and TouchDesigner projects on. Maybe somewhere around NW 16th & Johnson? 🤷🧐

📸: Terence Brasch

For International Women's Day, I'd like to highlight one of the most impactful humans to ever have touched my career: Tessa Ribitsch.

A little over five years ago, Tessa gave me a huge opportunity doing contract work at Downstream in a position I'm sure more qualified people also applied for. I don't know why she took a chance on me, but her generosity opened my eyes to an industry that I didn't know existed and that I would end up falling in love with.

Six months later, as the pandemic was in full-swing and I was sitting at home on my couch, she gave me another opportunity—this time an offer to be a full-time creative coder, all while knowing I didn't know a lick of C++ but also aware that I'd bust my tush to learn it. Her belief in my potential, not my portfolio, put me in a position where I was able to learn a lower level programming language, which eventually shed the imposter syndrome that I had been carrying around with me for years.

It's impossible to look at my work history and not see the direct impact Tessa has made on my career and my life. Without her, I wouldn't have ever worked at Deeplocal. Heck, I wouldn't have even known that this industry existed. And to be perfectly frank, I don't think I'd even be programming still. There's a good chance I'd be tomato farming if I wasn't working around and supporting creatives making cool shit.

Tessa, you're a rockstar, a ninja, a [insert dorky LinkedIn title here]... but simply put, I think you're a badass. I'm so happy that I was lucky enough to cross paths with you. Thank you for everything you've done over the years. 💪

This is what happens when a team only spends 10% (or some other arbitrary small amount of time) fixing technical debt.

This is what happens when you treat tech debt as some special, separate thing instead of a natural part of software development—a by-product of changing business needs and evolving software.

Tech debt isn’t an exceptional problem; it’s ordinary. Just like real infrastructure, it needs ongoing investment—not just an occasional “cleanup sprint” when things start breaking.

But when companies ignore it for too long, the system reaches what I call the Software Event Horizon—the point where the cost of making any change is so high that even the simplest features take forever, or result in bugs. And refactoring is impossible. There's no going back.

I wrote more about this in my article, "When to Throw in the Towel on Your Technical Debt". If you’ve ever seen a project slowly collapse under its own weight, you know exactly what I’m talking about.

Article: https://lnkd.in/gabpP-52

"What about this internet thing? Do you do you know anything about that?" 

“It's a place where people can publish information. They can have their own homepage, companies are there, the latest information."

This exchange went down in 1995 between David Letterman and Bill Gates. 
At the time, the conversation was met with skepticism. Dave even asked why anyone would bother listening to a baseball game on the computer when they have a radio.

Fast forward to now, and most people can't imagine not having the internet — and some have never known life without it.

That's because any time you're disrupting a product or industry, it takes time — and most importantly education — to change behaviors and opinions to onboard users. 

As a startup, we're tackling the challenge of how brands manage and measure their physical spaces (which FYI, hasn't changed much in YEARS). 

When they find out that Gumband lets you capture digital analytics for in-person environments — transforming them into measurable marketing assets — the immediate response is 👀 🤯 followed by "We've needed this, tell us more." 

Early adopters (Google, TikTok, Stripe, Nike, the NFL) use our platform to future-proof their interactive spaces, enhance user journeys, optimize the impact of their experiential investments and generate new insights while saving time and money.

We're a small and mighty team powering the future of experiential marketing because we believe that experiences matter and we can make them better. 

Connect with us to learn more, and comment with your favorite experiential memories.

The title for this video is pretty cringeworthy, but I think that the overall message is stellar: Make sure that you're always striving to be as hospitable as you possibly can. Like, to a ridiculous extreme.

The argument here is that if two different services are equivalent in almost every way, the differentiator might be how personalized of an experience the consumer is offered. You can't just give just good service - remember that the idea is to go beyond expectation. Leave your consumer with an experience they'll never forget.

Any service that's provided can benefit. Restaurants are the example that Will Guidara uses to lay the foundation for the discussion since it's probably what most of us think of when we think of hospitality, but this mentality could easily be applied to how you manage your people, how you interact with your coworkers, how you interact with folks online... you catch my drift.

This video is well worth the five minutes it takes to watch.

2023 was a freaking wild year for me. In a year of mass layoffs and job uncertainty, I chose to voluntarily leave my job so I could try to find what makes me happy at work and in life. Here are three HUGE lessons I learned last year:

💰 Money doesn't matter as much to me as it used to. Okay, I know that sounds grossly altruistic but here me out. I had always felt like I'd been behind where I "should be" as far as my salary goes, and this year was when I realized that, hey, it's not all about the Benjamins. Love what you do. Speaking of which...

🎨 What I'm working on matters to me. I need to be inspired by the products I build and support. Working in experiential technology was a blessing and I didn't realize how much I loved it until I left it to work in e-commerce. And about work...

🫣 Freelancing might not be for me. There, I said it. I'm so pumped that some people are able to do it successfully, but gosh darn is it hard, time consuming, and often thankless. Plus, I just don't want to make a website for your uncle's business.

In 2014, I was managing the front-of-house of a microbrewery in rural Pennsylvania trying to figure out where to go from there. Tomorrow I start a new job at a company that I've wanted to work at for years. What a life.

OpenAI's ChatGPT turns 1 today! 🎉 This got me thinking about how much it has impacted my life so far:

✅ It has made me a much better developer. Being able to pair program with an LLM that has extensive knowledge of best practices and has a solid understanding of programming is immensely valuable.

✅ It has made me a significantly more marketable job candidate. I was able to produce the best resume I've ever had by bouncing ideas off of it and comparing my skills with what jobs are looking for. 

✅ Finally, it has given me a new creative outlet. I love using it to generate images with DALL-E 3, write stories about ridiculous nonsense, and anything else I can think of to keep me occupied.

If there's one thing that I've learned, it's that it's ultimately still a tool and NOT a replacement. In other words, I don't assume that the code it writes is great, nor do I just take the resume advice that it gives me as gospel. In fact, a lot of times it's kinda crappy. However, I've learned how to use it as an intelligent, supremely well educated, and non-judgemental partner in a lot of the tasks that I do every single day.

Here's to the future. 🥂

Just came across this insightful guide on "Prompt Engineering" on freeCodeCamp that demystifies the art of communicating with AI. It highlights the importance of understanding how to craft effective prompts to enhance the quality and accuracy of AI responses.

Here are a few key takeaways: 

1️⃣ Prompt Engineering is a step-by-step process of creating inputs that guide the output generated by an AI language model. 

2️⃣ AI Language models like GPT-4 use deep learning algorithms and natural language processing (NLP) to understand human language. 

3️⃣ Different categories of prompts can be used to achieve various results, including information-seeking, instruction-based, context-providing, comparative, opinion-seeking, and reflective prompts. 

4️⃣ Role-based prompts are particularly useful, assigning a role to the AI model to provide responses within a specific context.
Remember, while AI has become remarkably sophisticated, it's not infallible. Always crosscheck the responses from AI models with other sources when in doubt.

I might be late to the party, but this is exciting: 
 
When I logged into WHM today, I was notified that Node.js 10 was now an installable package for Apache. From the research I've done in the past, it always seemed like Node *could* be installed, but it required some wizardry that also made it lose some of what makes Node great. Hence, I've had to stick to PHP since I live on the LAMP stack. Sad!

After installing it this morning, however, I couldn't be any happier. The only hiccup I've found was that the "node" command doesn't work immediately (you have to make a .bashrc alias to make it work). Once that's done, it's like butter.
